summary:
This change replaces repeated pop/unshift operations with three in-place reversals to rotate an array right.
- The function normalizes the rotation count and returns an empty array unchanged.
- It reverses the whole array, then reverses each of the two resulting groups.
- It changes and returns the same array.
riskRationale: This is a small refactor with no external dependencies. Review must check element order, rotation count normalization, and empty-array handling. No tests are supplied.
storyArc: The single topic follows the same elements through three reversals. It shows how the first reversal exchanges the two groups, while the next two reversals restore order within each group.

topics.title: Rotate right with three in-place reversals
topics.narrativeBrief: Use [A,B,C,D,E] with k = 2 to explain why each reversal is necessary. Keep element identity visible through all three phases, and state the empty-array and rotation count rules separately.

diagramBrief.question: How do the three reversals move [D,E] before [A,B,C] and restore order within both groups?
diagramBrief.takeaway: The array changes from [A,B,C,D,E] to [E,D,C,B,A], then [D,E,C,B,A], then [D,E,A,B,C]. Both groups finish in their original internal order.
assumedKnowledge: A reversal exchanges elements from opposite ends of a range.
essentialConcepts: All reversals change the same array.
The normalized rotation count is 2 for this example.
The whole-array reversal exchanges group positions and reverses order within both groups.
The first group reversal covers indices 0 through k - 1.
The second group reversal covers indices k through items.length - 1.
An empty array returns before rotation count normalization.
Normalization maps negative and oversized integer counts into the array's index range.
omit: A separate diagram of repeated pop/unshift operations
A walkthrough of every loop iteration
diagramBrief.visualApproach: Use an animated SVG execution walkthrough with one fixed row of five indexed positions. Give [A,B,C] and [D,E] distinct group colors, and keep each letter visible as its position changes. Show the three reversal ranges in sequence, with a pause after each phase and a small record of each completed state. Position means array index; color means original group membership. This form is better than a static relationship map because the difficult point is the movement of the same elements, not a dependency. The animation shows both groups change position during the whole-array reversal, then recover their internal order during separate reversals. Keep the k = 2 boundary visible after the first phase. State normalization and the empty-array return in nearby text rather than adding unrelated branches to this example.
